questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. Inguinal lymph nodes are non-tender and rubbery. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows corkscrew-motility organisms. What is the drug of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Drug of choice is benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose. Doxycycline is used in penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a verrucous plaque on the dorsum of the foot with black dots on the surface. Skin biopsy shows 'Medlar bodies' (sclerotic cells). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is characterised by verrucous plaques with black dots (caused by transepidermal elimination of fungi). Histopathology shows pathognomonic Medlar bodies (muriform/sclerotic cells) which are thick-walled, brown, septate fungal cells.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. The lesions started as vesicles that ruptured. Gram stain of crust shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (sometimes mixed with Streptococcus pyogenes). The honey-coloured crust is classical. Bullous impetigo is exclusively caused by S. aureus phage type 71.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with grouped tense vesicles on an erythematous base on the lip, recurring every few months triggered by fever. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What type of hypersensitivity is involved in erythema multiforme that can follow this infection?
questions.exp: Herpes simplex virus-associated erythema multiforme is mediated by Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity. HSV DNA fragments are deposited in skin, and HSV-specific CD4+ T cells and interferon-gamma mediate keratinocyte apoptosis.

questions.q: A borderline tuberculoid leprosy patient develops sudden painful erythema and swelling of existing skin patches with neuritis. ESR is elevated; no new bacilli are seen. What is this reaction and first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction occurs in borderline leprosy. It is a Type IV (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction manifesting as acute inflammation of existing lesions with neuritis. First-line treatment is prednisolone starting at 40 mg/day, tapered over 3–6 months.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with photosensitive erythema on the face in a butterfly distribution, discoid plaques, oral ulcers, and alopecia. ANA is positive (1:640, homogeneous pattern). Which antibody is most specific for this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific antibody for SLE (specificity ~99%), though not very sensitive (~25%). Anti-dsDNA is also specific but less so. Anti-histone is for drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro is for neonatal lupus and Sjögren's.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with flaccid bullae on apparently normal skin that rupture easily leaving erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG deposition in a 'fishnet/chicken wire' pattern within the epidermis. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris involves flaccid blisters on mucosa and skin with intraepidermal splitting at the suprabasal level. The target antigen is Desmoglein 3 (mucosal type) and sometimes Desmoglein 1+3 (mucocutaneous type). DIF shows IgG in an intercellular 'fishnet' pattern.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with tense bullae on the trunk and flexures, with intense pruritus. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the ultrastructural location of the split?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid shows tense subepidermal blisters. The split occurs in the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. Target antigens are BP180 (collagen XVII, NC16A domain) and BP230. DIF shows linear IgG/C3 at the DEJ.

questions.q: A 60-year-old female presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasia on the nose that has been slowly enlarging over 2 years. Dermoscopy shows arborising vessels. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for a 1 cm lesion on this anatomical site?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma on the nose (H-zone of the face) is a high-risk location with increased recurrence rates. Mohs micrographic surgery is the treatment of choice for high-risk BCC as it provides complete margin control with maximum tissue sparing.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with HIV (CD4 count 80/µL) presents with multiple red-violet papules and nodules on the skin and oral mucosa. Histopathology shows proliferating spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and HHV-8 positive cells. What is the most appropriate systemic treatment?
questions.exp: AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma caused by HHV-8. For widespread/visceral disease, liposomal doxorubicin (first-line chemotherapy) combined with ART is standard. ART alone can cause KS regression in mild cases but systemic disease requires chemotherapy.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with well-defined, silvery-white scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees. A new plaque has appeared at the site of a recent scratch. Which phenomenon does this represent and which cytokine is central to its pathogenesis?
questions.exp: New plaque at a site of trauma represents the Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon, characteristic of psoriasis. IL-17 (from Th17 cells) is the key downstream effector cytokine driving psoriatic inflammation and keratinocyte proliferation. IL-23 drives Th17 differentiation upstream.

questions.q: A 25-year-old atopic individual presents with intensely pruritic, vesicular, and weeping dermatitis in the antecubital fossae and popliteal fossae. Serum IgE is elevated. Skin biopsy shows spongiosis. Which finding best differentiates atopic dermatitis from contact dermatitis histologically?
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis and allergic contact dermatitis are histologically indistinguishable. Both show spongiosis and lymphocytic infiltrate. Differentiation requires clinical history, patch testing (for contact dermatitis), and IgE levels. Histology alone is insufficient.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with multiple hypopigmented, anaesthetic macules on the trunk. Slit-skin smear from the most active edge of a lesion shows 2+ bacillary index. Nerve biopsy shows granulomas with no bacilli. What is the WHO classification and treatment?
opts: Multibacillary; Dapsone + Rifampicin + Clofazimine for 12 months
questions.exp: A bacillary index of 2+ from any site classifies the patient as multibacillary leprosy regardless of clinical features. WHO-MDT for multibacillary leprosy: Rifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg daily + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly (supervised) and 50 mg daily for 12 months.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, calcinosis, and telangiectasias. Barium swallow shows oesophageal dysmotility. ANA is positive with centromere pattern. What is this syndrome and its associated antibody?
opts: Mixed connective tissue disease; anti-U1 RNP
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is a limited form of systemic sclerosis. It is strongly associated with anti-centromere antibody (ACA), which gives a centromere ANA pattern. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis.

questions.q: A 19-year-old male presents with a solitary painless genital ulcer that is clean-based with firm (indurated) margins and a satellite lymph node that is non-tender. Serology for syphilis is non-reactive on day 5 of illness. Which additional test should be ordered to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.exp: In primary syphilis, serological tests (VDRL, RPR) may be non-reactive in the first 1–2 weeks. Dark-field microscopy of serous exudate from the ulcer base directly visualises Treponema pallidum (corkscrew motility), making it the test of choice in early primary syphilis before seroconversion.

questions.q: A patient with tinea capitis showing a large boggy, tender, fluctuant mass on the scalp with multiple pustules and crusting is diagnosed with kerion celsi. What is the preferred treatment and why should topical antifungals be avoided?
opts: Oral griseofulvin; topicals do not penetrate the hair follicle
Topical ketoconazole; systemic therapy has more side effects
questions.exp: Tinea capitis (including kerion) requires systemic antifungal therapy because the infection is within the hair follicle and shaft, which topical agents cannot reach. Griseofulvin is the traditional first-line drug (particularly effective against Microsporum spp.). Oral terbinafine is preferred for Trichophyton species.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with red-brown atrophic macules with 'cigarette paper' wrinkling on the trunk and axillae. Biopsy shows loss of elastic fibres in the mid-dermis with normal epidermis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mid-dermal elastolysis presents with fine wrinkled macules due to loss of elastic fibres specifically in the mid-dermis (unlike anetoderma which affects the superficial/mid dermis with protrusion, or cutis laxa which is widespread). The cigarette-paper wrinkling over the trunk is characteristic.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive male (not on ART) develops multiple discrete, dome-shaped, flesh-coloured papules with central umbilication across the face, trunk, and genitalia. CD4 count is 90/µL. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Initiate ART; lesions will regress with immune reconstitution
Initiate ART and perform physical destruction of lesions
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum in HIV with low CD4 count is widespread and recalcitrant. ART is essential for immune reconstitution (CD4 recovery leads to spontaneous regression). Physical destruction (curettage, cryotherapy, or laser) of lesions should also be performed alongside ART for faster clearance.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery, frozen sections are cut at a specific angle to examine the deep and peripheral margins simultaneously. What percentage of margins are evaluated with conventional bread-loaf sections versus Mohs surgery?
questions.exp: Conventional histopathology (bread-loaf technique) samples only 1–2% of the surgical margin, so tumour at unsampled margins can be missed. Mohs micrographic surgery evaluates 100% of the surgical margin by horizontally cutting tissue in a manner that maps the entire undersurface and peripheral edges.

questions.q: A patient on long-term dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia. Which enzyme deficiency significantly increases the risk of these side effects?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in all patients, but these effects are dramatically worsened in G6PD-deficient individuals. G6PD testing is essential before starting dapsone. In G6PD deficiency, reduced glutathione cannot protect erythrocytes from oxidative stress caused by dapsone hydroxylamine metabolites.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a slowly growing, painless, darkly pigmented macule on the sole of the foot with irregular borders and variegated pigmentation. Dermoscopy reveals a parallel ridge pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) on the sole shows the pathognomonic parallel ridge pattern on dermoscopy (pigmentation along the ridges of the dermatoglyphics, not the furrows). Benign melanocytic naevi show a parallel furrow pattern. ALM is the most common melanoma subtype in Asian populations.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with SLE is started on hydroxychloroquine. What baseline investigation and monitoring is mandatory before and during this therapy?
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinopathy (bull's eye maculopathy) with long-term use. Baseline ophthalmologic examination is mandatory before starting therapy. Annual retinal screening is recommended (more frequent if risk factors like daily dose >5 mg/kg, >5 years of use, or renal/hepatic disease).

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with asymptomatic, flesh-coloured, filiform warts around the beard area that recur despite cryotherapy. Histology shows koilocytes and papillomatosis. HPV typing shows HPV type 2. Which treatment modality is specifically indicated for plane warts on the face?
questions.exp: Plane (flat) warts on the face are best treated with topical retinoids (tretinoin) due to their anti-proliferative effect on keratinocytes. Salicylic acid at high concentrations and cantharidin/bleomycin are more suitable for plantar warts. Retinoids are safe and effective for facial plane warts.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with a 30-year history of psoriasis develops swollen, sausage-shaped fingers and deformity of the distal interphalangeal joints with nail changes (oil-drop sign, pitting). X-ray shows 'pencil-in-cup' deformity. What is the biologic drug class of choice for severe psoriatic arthritis?
questions.exp: Anti-TNF-α agents (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) are the first-line biologics for psoriatic arthritis as they target both skin and joint disease effectively. IL-17 inhibitors are highly effective for skin disease and also approved for PsA. IL-23 inhibitors are primarily for skin. Dupilumab is for atopic dermatitis.

questions.q: A 24-year-old sexually active male presents with multiple cauliflower-like verrucous papules on the coronal sulcus and perianal region. Acetowhitening test is positive. Which HPV types are most commonly responsible and what is the risk of malignant transformation?
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts) are most commonly caused by HPV types 6 and 11, which are considered low-risk (low oncogenic potential). High-risk types (HPV 16, 18) are associated with cervical and anogenital carcinomas. HPV 6/11 rarely cause malignant transformation.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with loss of pigment in a perioral distribution, over the knuckles, and around the eyes in a depigmented macule with confetti-like lesions at the margins. Wood's lamp shows chalk-white fluorescence. What finding on examination would suggest activity of this disease?
questions.exp: Vitiligo shows the Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon — new depigmented lesions developing at sites of trauma (scratching, pressure, burns), indicating active disease. Trichrome vitiligo and confetti depigmentation also suggest activity. Darier's sign is seen in mastocytosis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with a subcutaneous swelling on the nape of the neck. Excision biopsy shows a tumour with a capsule, proliferating adipocytes with no cytologic atypia, and occasional interspersed spindle cells. Fibrous septae are present. What is this lesion and what is its malignant counterpart?
questions.exp: Lipoma is the most common benign soft tissue tumour, typically on the neck and shoulders. Spindle cell lipoma contains spindle cells and CD34+ stroma but is still benign. The malignant counterpart of lipoma is liposarcoma. Spindle cell lipoma has deletion of 13q and 16q but remains benign.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male with chronic venous ulcers and lower limb oedema is prescribed graduated compression therapy. What is the recommended ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI) below which compression bandaging is contraindicated?
questions.exp: Graduated compression is the cornerstone of venous ulcer treatment. However, if ABPI < 0.8, significant arterial insufficiency is present and full-compression bandaging is contraindicated as it may compromise arterial blood flow. ABPI 0.8–1.0 warrants modified compression; ABPI > 1.0 allows full compression.

questions.q: A neonate presents at 3 weeks of age with erythematous papules and pustules on the cheeks and forehead. Examination reveals no comedones. The mother reports recent breastfeeding. KOH preparation of a pustule shows Malassezia spores. What is the diagnosis and management?
opts: Neonatal cephalic pustulosis; reassurance, topical ketoconazole if persistent
questions.exp: Neonatal cephalic pustulosis (formerly called neonatal acne) is associated with Malassezia colonisation and presents in the first weeks of life with papules and pustules without comedones. It is self-limiting; topical ketoconazole 2% cream is used if persistent. True neonatal acne is rare and linked to hormonal stimulation.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic, grouped, erythematous papulovesicles on the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp. Biopsy of a perilesional area shows granular IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. What systemic association must be screened for?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring disease) shows granular IgA deposits at the DEJ (pathognomonic) and is associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) in virtually all patients. Anti-endomysial and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are positive. A gluten-free diet is the primary treatment.
